Z01.concept: Zero to one, or one to n
Z01.task: Is your idea a 0-to-1 or a 1-to-n idea? Answer Thiel’s question for its area in one sentence. Judge: if it’s 1 to n, what do you do that the ones you copy don’t? If you can’t name it, that’s the first gap. Try it this week: find the three closest products to your idea and write what each one gets wrong.

l: Calling a copy new.
Copying with no reason to win: the same product, for the same people, with a smaller budget.

walk.h: Worked: an app like Intensity Applied
p: An app for lifters who want to build muscle is 1 to n: training apps and logbooks already exist. That’s fine. The work is the gap: a group the big apps serve badly, such as lifters who have stalled for months, and the one thing done for them that the others don’t do.

l: One word first: ‘1 to n’, for most first products.
One sentence naming a group and a gap, e.g. ‘lifters who’ve stalled for months get generic programmes; nobody shows them which variable to change next’.
Three named competitors, each with one specific miss taken from a user’s complaint (an app review, a forum post), not from your guess.

Z01.rtask: Your idea: 0 to 1 or 1 to n, and the one thing it would do that the closest product doesn’t.

l: Most are 1 to n. The answer is one specific gap for one group, taken from a real complaint about the closest product; if you can’t name one, that’s the finding.

Z02.task: Which of the four could your idea have in five years — honestly? Name it, and what you’d have to do from day one to build it. Judge: if a funded competitor copied your idea next month, what would they still not have? Try it this week: write that answer as your one-line pitch.

l: Calling ‘first’ a moat: Thiel argues the last mover wins.
A brand with nothing underneath it.

walk.h: Worked: an app like Intensity Applied
l: Technology 10 times better is hard: most training logic is public.
Network effects are weak, unless many lifters’ data makes the advice better for each one.
Scale: software is cheap to serve, but so is every rival’s.
So the likeliest moat is that data, built from day one by logging what each lifter changed and what happened next.
One moat, chosen honestly. ‘None yet’ is fine if you name the one you’ll build.
A day-one action that starts it: logging the data, starting the community, owning the niche’s name.
The copycat line, written as your one-line pitch: what they’d still lack next month.

Z02.rtask: Your idea: which moat could it build, and what’s the first step this month?

l: One of Thiel’s four, or Hormozi’s know-how, with a concrete first step. ‘None yet’ counts if you name the one you’ll build.

Z03.task: Write your idea’s smallest real market in one sentence: who, doing what, where. Roughly how many of them are there, and how would you reach the first 100? Judge: is it small enough that you’d be their obvious choice, but big enough to matter? Try it this week: message three people in that group.

l: The 1% of a huge market.
A group so broad that no single place reaches it.
Skipping the market tests: pain, money, easy to find, growing.

p: PayPal didn’t start with everyone who pays online. It started with eBay’s power sellers: a small group who traded every day and talked to each other. Once they used it, the rest of eBay followed. Thiel’s rule: dominate a small market, then expand to the one next to it.

l: Who, doing what, where, e.g. ‘lifters training 3–5 times a week who’ve stalled for six months, in strength-training communities online’.
A rough count with its source, like a community’s member count or an association’s list. A guess with a source beats a big number without one.
A plan for the first 100 that names the place and the message, not ‘social media’.

Z03.rtask: Your idea: its smallest real market in one sentence, and where the first 100 gather.

l: Who, doing what, where, in one sentence, plus a named place where they gather. If the place is ‘online’, the group is still too broad.

Z07.concept: If you build it, they won’t just come
Z07.task: Make a distribution map for your idea: 20 places its customers already pay attention — subreddits, creators, newsletters, groups, search terms, tools they pay for. Pick one channel for the first 100 users. Judge: what will one customer cost you there, and what will they pay you in a year? Try it this week: post or reply once in that channel.

l: Posting everywhere instead of doing one channel well.
A €5-a-month app, sold one person at a time.

walk.h: Worked: an app at €5 a month
p: A user who stays 6 months is worth €30. Winning each one by hand, even 30 minutes at your €40 an hour, costs €20: only 1.5 times, in the doldrums. So the channel has to be nearly free per user: a community where one post reaches thousands, or users who bring other users.

l: 20 named places, not categories: that subreddit, that newsletter, that creator, that search phrase.
One channel and why: the group already talks about the problem there, in its own words.
Two numbers: the cost to win one customer there, and a year’s revenue from one. The second should be at least three times the first; at €5 a month that means winning each user for under €20.

Z07.rtask: Your idea: one channel for the first 100, what a customer costs you there, and what one pays you in a year.

l: A year’s revenue should be at least three times what one customer costs to win. At a low monthly price, the channel has to be nearly free per user.

Z08.concept: Score it, pick one, set a kill rule
Z08.task: Score every idea you’re weighing, Intensity Applied and any others, on the seven questions. Pick the one to test next, and write the result that would make you drop it — for example, fewer than 3 of 10 people commit. Judge: is your favourite also the best-scoring one? If not, why? Try it this week: run its test.

l: Scoring your favourite generously.
No kill rule, so nothing ever fails and nothing gets dropped.

p: Thiel blames the cleantech crash of the late 2000s on companies that answered few of the seven well: no clearly better technology, bad timing, crowded markets, weak sales, no secret. Solyndra is the main example in the book.

l: A table of ideas × the seven, yes or no (or 1–5), with the weakest question for each idea named.
The pick, and if it isn’t the top score, the reason in one line.
A kill rule with a number and a date: e.g. ‘fewer than 3 of 10 pay for the founding year within six weeks: drop it’.

Z08.rtask: Your idea: score it on the seven questions and write its kill rule.

l: Seven answers with the weakest one named, and a kill rule with a number and a date, written before the test.

M01.concept: Ask about their life, not your idea
M01.task: Write three bad questions and three good ones for your idea, then rewrite each bad one into a good one. Judge: which good question is most likely to show you you’re wrong? Try it this week: ask it to two real people, and note who they were and what you learned.

l: Pitching and calling it research.
Counting compliments as demand.

p: Its founders ran about 20 of these calls a week, about 2,000 in all, and found their product in what people already did: they narrowed an all-in-one tool down to one job. It reached $69K a month within two months.
walk.s: Starter Story · How This SaaS Hit $69K/Month In Just 2 Months

l: Good questions start with ‘the last time’, ‘walk me through’, ‘what have you tried’, ‘what did it cost’. For Intensity Applied: ‘When did your lifts last go up? What did you change after that?’
Bad ones mention the product or ask about the future: ‘Would you pay for an app that…’.
The one most likely to prove you wrong: ‘What have you tried to fix it?’ If the answer is ‘nothing’, the pain may not be real.

M01.rtask: Your idea: one bad question rewritten into a good one, and the question most likely to prove you wrong.

l: The good version asks about a specific past event (‘the last time…’). The riskiest question is usually ‘what have you tried?’: no attempts, no real pain.

M02.task: Take three reactions you’ve had to your idea — or typical ones: “Nice!”, “I’d use that”, “It should have X”. Sort each into compliment, fluff or idea, and write the follow-up question that turns it into a fact. Judge: what’s the one fact about your customer you still don’t know? Try it this week: get that fact from one person.

l: Leaving on a high with nothing written down.
Building the requested feature instead of finding the reason behind it.

walk.h: Worked: three reactions, turned into facts
l: ‘Nice idea!’ is a compliment: ‘Thanks. How do you handle it today?’
‘I’d use that every week’ is fluff: ‘When did you last need it? What did you do?’
‘It should sync with my watch’ is a request: ‘What would that let you do that you can’t now?’
Each reaction labelled, then followed by a question about the past or about why.
The missing fact is about their life, not your product. For Intensity Applied, e.g.: how many lifters who stall actually change anything, and what.
Getting it from one person this week counts. A survey of opinions doesn’t.

M02.rtask: Your idea: the most common compliment or ‘I would’ you’ve heard, and the question that turns it into a fact.

l: Anchor it in the past: ‘When did that last happen? What did you do?’ A fact is something that already happened, with a cost or a time attached.

M04.task: For your idea, write the commitment you’ll ask for at each stage: after a first chat, after a demo, and before you build the full product. Judge: what’s the smallest money commitment that would really prove demand? Try it this week: ask one person for it.

l: Not asking, to keep the meeting pleasant.
Treating ‘sounds great, keep me posted’ as a yes.

p: Cleo built a waitlist from LinkedIn posts and sold its paid beta only to that list: about $30K a month within days, before any public launch. Joining the waitlist cost people time; the paid beta cost money.
walk.s: Starter Story · How My App Hit $60K/Month in 2 Months

l: Three asks, one per stage, each one something they could say no to.
A real, small money ask. For Intensity Applied, e.g.: a founding-member year at a discount, paid before launch, offered only to the waitlist.
The result that would stop you, in numbers, decided now: e.g. fewer than 3 of 10 people who saw the demo pay.

M04.rtask: Your idea: the smallest money commitment that would prove demand, and the result that would stop you.

l: A real payment they could refuse: a pre-order, a deposit, a paid beta. The stopping result is a number decided now, e.g. fewer than 3 of 10.

M05.task: Write your idea’s first-100 plan: who is already searching for a solution, one thing that doesn’t scale you’d do for each early user, and where you’ll show up. Judge: which step gets you the first 10, and how fast? Try it this week: do the unscalable thing for one person.

l: Waiting for a launch day.
Automating something before you’ve done it by hand ten times.

p: Its founder talked to more than 100 founders before building, then made free demos for founders who asked on Reddit, in public, so others saw them. It is now at $250K a month.
walk.s: Starter Story · How This $250K/Month SaaS Got Its First 100 Users (Steal This Playbook)

l: For Intensity Applied, e.g.: lifters searching ‘plateau’ or ‘stalled bench press’ (searchers); a free review of someone’s last eight weeks of training, posted with permission (unscalable, and public); the communities on your distribution map (show up).
The first 10 usually come from the unscalable step: one person at a time, starting this week.
A date for the first 10, and what you’ll do if they aren’t in by then.

M05.rtask: Your idea: one thing that doesn’t scale you’d do for each of the first 10 users.

l: Something personal and visible: a free review, a done-with-you setup, a reply in public. If it takes more than an hour each, make it smaller, not automated.
